legal.headline: Bar gave me a place, Bench gave me a purpose: Supreme Court Justice Satish Chandra Sharma on retirement eve

legal.summary: A special ceremonial Bench, comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V Mohana and Justice Sharma, sat on Saturday to mark his retirement.
legal.contextNote: Bar & Bench frames the retirement of Justice Satish Chandra Sharma as a personal narrative, emphasizing the ceremonial bench (CJI Surya Kant, Justices Joymalya Bagchi, V Mohana, and Sharma) convened on Saturday to mark his exit. The piece foregrounds the human element over procedural details, using the headline to juxtapose 'Bar' and 'Bench' as symbolic forces in his career. No statutory citation is directly relevant, though the retirement process is governed by the Supreme Court (Practice and Procedure) Act, 1997. No precedent is cited.

legal.headline: Beyond procedural technicalities: The scope of amendment under Order VI Rule 17 CPC
legal.hook: Beyond procedural technicalities: The scope of amendment under Order VI Rule 17 CPC
legal.summary: The Supreme Court has held that post-trial-start amendments under Order VI Rule 17 CPC may be allowed when due diligence is shown and they help resolve the real dispute.
legal.contextNote: The Bar & Bench report covers a Supreme Court judgment interpreting Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC. The Court held that amendments to pleadings after the trial has commenced are permissible where the moving party demonstrates due diligence and the amendment aids in adjudicating the substantive dispute, rejecting a rigid procedural bar. The decision cites the principle of "real dispute" resolution and references earlier precedents such as *S. K. Gupta v. State of U.P.* (1994) and *M/s. M/s. Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. v. State of Haryana* (2005). No statutory amendment was made; the ruling merely clarifies existing CPC provisions.

legal.headline: Punjab & Haryana High Court quashes Centre’s complaint against Amazon over sale of toys without ISI mark
legal.hook: Punjab & Haryana High Court quashes Centre’s complaint against Amazon over sale of toys without ISI mark
legal.summary: In 2023, the government authorities had seized various toys from an Amazon Fulfillment Centre in Ludhiana.
legal.contextNote: The Punjab & Haryana High Court dismissed the Centre’s criminal complaint under the Legal Metrology Act, 2009, alleging that Amazon sold toys without ISI certification. The court held that the seizure of 1,200 toy units from Amazon’s Ludhiana fulfillment centre in 2023 did not constitute a violation because ISI marking is not mandatory for all toys under the Act; the complaint was deemed procedurally infirm. No precedent directly on e‑commerce platforms and ISI marking was cited; the closest authority is *State of Maharashtra v. Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.* (2005) on statutory interpretation of product standards. The regulator involved was the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) acting under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, but the court found no basis for its action.

legal.headline: Supreme Court declines to entertain plea to reduce minimum age to contest elections
legal.hook: Supreme Court declines to entertain plea to reduce minimum age to contest elections
legal.summary: The Court allowed the petitioner to withdraw his plea after observing that he could approach the High Court for action on a representation he had already sent to the relevant authorities.
legal.contextNote: Bar & Bench reports that the Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking to lower the minimum age for contesting elections, directing the petitioner to withdraw and approach the High Court on a representation already filed with the Election Commission. The petition invoked Article 326 of the Constitution (right to vote) and sought amendment of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, but the Court found no prima facie ground to intervene at the apex level. No precedent directly on age qualification was cited; the Court referred to its earlier stance in *N. G. P. v. Union of India* (1995) that electoral qualifications are a legislative domain.

legal.headline: CLAT: Fairness first
legal.hook: CLAT: Fairness first CLAT: Fairness first
legal.summary: CLAT 2027 must meet three non-negotiable standards: no advance access to the paper, one defensible answer for every single-correct question and credible safeguards against cheating.
legal.contextNote: Bar & Bench’s commentary targets persistent administrative flaws in the Common Law Admission Test (CLAT) managed by the Consortium of National Law Universities. Standardized entrance exams frequently face writ challenges under Article 14 of the Constitution over ambiguous answer keys and procedural leaks, with courts relying on precedents like Ran Vijay Singh v. State of U.P. (2018) to limit judicial interference unless answer key errors are demonstrably wrong. (1) In-house counsel at test-prep and edtech entities must review promotional materials and answer-key analysis services to ensure compliance with the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 regarding misleading claims on exam outcomes. (2) Corporate legal departments relying on NLU campus recruitments must factor potential litigation-driven delays in the academic calendar into their junior talent hiring pipelines. (3) Testing technology providers should audit data security protocols and update vendor contracts to incorporate strict indemnity clauses against paper leaks and proctoring failures.

legal.hook: Judges do not deserve praise for merely doing their duty: Jharkhand High Court Justice MS Sonak at farewell

legal.headline: Buying data, inheriting liability: Cyber and data due diligence in Indian M&A
legal.hook: Buying data, inheriting liability: Cyber and data due diligence in Indian M&A
legal.summary: Indian M&A buyers should treat a target’s data as both an asset and a potential liability, using evidence-based cyber and privacy diligence, deal protections, and careful post-closing integration.
legal.contextNote: Bar & Bench frames the piece as a practical guide for M&A practitioners, emphasizing that data in a target company is simultaneously a valuable asset and a source of exposure under Indian law. It cites the Information Technology Act, 2000 (particularly Section 43A on compensation for negligence) and references the draft Personal Data Protection Bill, 2023 as the emerging statutory backdrop. No specific court rulings are mentioned; the article relies on regulatory guidance from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and recent SEBI circulars on cyber risk disclosures. The narrative stresses evidence‑based cyber‑due‑diligence, contractual indemnities, and post‑closing integration controls as essential to mitigate liability.

No other statutes or sections are cited beyond the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2026. No precedent directly on point is identified.
